Acute Liver Failure

Liver functions

  • Liver is responsible for
  • Detoxification
  • Support metabolism
  • Immunity
  • Digestion
  • Synthesis of protein such as albumin, coagulation factors…

Definition

  • Acute liver failure should have all of these elements to be considered acute liver failure :
  • Severe acute liver injury (hepatocyte necrosis)
  • Duration is less than 26 weeks
  • Evidence of encephalopathy: DLOC, change in behavior
  • Impaired Synthetic function of the liver: abnormal coagulation profile (INR ≥ 1.5)
  • The patient should not have liver cirrhosis or pre existing liver disease

Causes

  • When patient present with acute liver failure, think of liver diseases that cause a lot of damage in short period of time
  • Drug induced hepatitis due to paracetamol ingestion (first most common)
  • Viral hepatitis (second most common)
  • Shocked liver (ischemia or hypoxia)
  • Budd Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis)
  • Veno occlusive disease
  • Mushroom ingestion
  • Wilsons disease
  • Sepsis
  • Autoimmune hepatitis
  • Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
  • HELLP syndrome
  • Heat stroke
  • Malignant infiltration
  • Slow progressive liver diseases don’t cause acute liver failure, but rather cause chronic liver failure
  • NAFLD
  • Hemochromatosis
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis
  • Primary biliary cirrhosis
  • Alpha 1 antitrypsin deficiency

Pathophysiology

  • Most causes lead to hepatocyte ATP depletion and cellular swelling => cell membrane disruption
  • Massive hepatocyte necrosis and apoptosis => liver failure

Signs and Symptoms

  • Fatigue, weakness
  • Confusion because of hepatic encephalopathy
  • Jaundice due to hyperbilirubinemia
  • Hepatomegaly (liver congestion)
  • Abdominal pain especially right upper quadrant
  • Abnormal LFTs
  • Abnormal coagulation profile, elevated PT/PTT
  • Thrombocytopenia due to loss of TPO

Medical history

  • Comprehensive history helps to exclude DDX, ask for:
  • Timeline of symptoms and progression
  • Any history of hepatic disease
  • Drug history looking for acetaminophen toxicity
  • Family history looking for Wilson disease and thrombotic disorders
  • Any recent surgeries looking for possible toxic medications used like some anesthetic agents

Examination

  • Check vitals looking for hypotension (sepsis)
  • Abdominal palpation looking for pain and tenderness
  • Special tests looking for ascites
  • Altered mental status
  • Fever (infection)

Diagnosis

  • Requirements to diagnose Acute liver failure
  • Evidence of liver injury: Elevated AST/ALT
  • Evidence of hepatic encephalopathy: change in behavior, decreased level of consciousness, coma
  • INR more or equal to 1.5
  • Follow up investigations
  • Look for hypoglycemia
  • Look for hyperbilirubinemia
  • Low PLT
  • US to look for Budd Chiari syndrome
  • Look for acute kidney injury (elevated urea and creatinine)
  • Electrolyte abnormalities
  • Abdominal imaging looking for cirrhosis, features of portal hypertension, hepatocellular carcinoma, vascular problems

Histopathology

  • Done only if the cause didn’t get identified through history, examination, investigations
  • Trans jugular liver biopsy taken and examined

Management - Definitive management

  • Admit to ICU
  • If you already know the cause then treat the cause
  • If you don’t know the cause then give N acetylcysteine (paracetamol antidote) and then you can look for the cause
  • Treat the identified cause
  • Liver transplantation if treatment not succeeded

Management - Supportive management

  • IV fluid with controlling acid base balance and electrolytes
  • Monitor for any bleeding (patient have coagulopathy) and treat with blood products
  • Blood and urine cultures and start empirical antibiotics if patient have fever
  • Monitor hepatic encephalopathy and protect airway
  • Provide nutrition
  • Monitor for hypoglycemia and maintain blood glucose between 160- 200

Complication

Renal failure

Sepsis

Hypoglycemia

  • Cerebral edema (most common cause of death in ALF) : edema lead to intracranial hypertension, ischemic brain injury and herniation, triggers include hypoxia, hypotension, decreased cerebral perfusion and increased ammonia levels

Complications

Encephalopathy

Coagulopathy
